title: Pooling and spatial information
goals: Compute max and mean pooling under an explicit window rule
Use collisions to explain lost spatial information
Test boundary and movement claims with revealing examples

prerequisite.prompt: For a 3 by 3 input and a 2 by 2 window with stride 2 and no padding, how many valid window positions exist?
prerequisite.answer: Only the start at row 0 column 0 fits. The output shape is 1 by 1 under the complete-window rule.

vocabulary: Replacing each window by its largest value
Replacing each window by the arithmetic mean of its values
Information about where values occur and how positions relate
Different inputs producing the same pooled values

blocks.text: A fictional single-channel feature map has rows [1, 4, 2, 0], [3, 2, 5, 1], [0, 6, 1, 3] and [2, 4, 2, 7]. Use a 2 by 2 window, stride 2, no padding and only complete windows. Coordinates are zero-based. The four starts are [0, 0], [0, 2], [2, 0] and [2, 2].

Max pooling keeps the largest value in each window. Mean pooling adds the four values and divides by 4. Neither operation learns weights in this lesson. These are fixed summaries of the incoming feature map, unlike the trainable kernel parameters introduced last week.

The max output is [[4, 5], [6, 7]], and the mean output is [[2.5, 2], [3, 3.25]]. Both have shape 2 by 2. Sixteen values become four, but the four outputs still preserve the coarse arrangement of the four regions.

This code assumes a nonempty rectangular numeric map at least 2 by 2. It uses only complete 2 by 2 windows, stride 2 and no padding. It returns two separate summaries of the same map; it does not apply one pooling operation after the other.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def pool2(image):
    h, w = len(image), len(image[0])
    if h < 2 or w < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need a complete 2 by 2 window")
    maxima, means = [], []
    for r in range(0, h - 1, 2):
        max_row, mean_row = [], []
        for c in range(0, w - 1, 2):
            values = [image[r+i][c+j]
                      for i in range(2) for j in range(2)]
            max_row.append(max(values))
            mean_row.append(sum(values) / 4)
        maxima.append(max_row)
        means.append(mean_row)
    return maxima, means

x = [[1, 4, 2, 0], [3, 2, 5, 1],
     [0, 6, 1, 3], [2, 4, 2, 7]]
assert pool2(x) == ([[4, 5], [6, 7]],
                    [[2.5, 2], [3, 3.25]])

For this complete-window rule the output shape is floor((H - 2) / 2) + 1 by floor((W - 2) / 2) + 1. A 3 by 3 map produces just one output; its last row and last column are not read. Do not silently invent a partial-window rule or pad missing positions.

lesson.title: Find different inputs with the same summary

blocks.title: A maximum does not identify its location
blocks.caption: The first two windows differ in the position of their nonzero value yet have the same maximum and mean. The third has the same maximum but a different mean. Each summary retains some distinctions and discards others.

blocks.label: Compare windows [[0, 0], [6, 0]] and [[0, 0], [0, 6]]. Compute both summaries. Can a deterministic head receiving only either scalar distinguish bottom-left from bottom-right?

blocks.text: Within one isolated window, rearranging its values preserves both its maximum and mean. But moving a value across a window boundary can change the output map. In a 2 by 4 map of zeros, put a single 8 at row 0 column 1. Max pooling gives [[8, 0]]. Move that 8 one column right to column 2, replacing the old position with zero: the output becomes [[0, 8]]. Pooling therefore does not guarantee that a classifier ignores every small movement.

Negative values are valid inputs. For [[-4, -2], [-7, -3]], the maximum is -2 and the mean is -4. Starting a maximum calculation at zero would incorrectly return 0. Adding a zero to the window would also change its maximum: padding choices matter. Our examples use no padding.

Returning the position of a maximum can preserve extra location information, but it still does not restore the discarded values. For example, [[5, 1], [2, 3]] and [[5, 0], [0, 0]] have the same unique maximum 5 at the top-left position. Even the maximum plus its position cannot tell which original window was used.

Pooling can reduce the amount of data processed by later layers. Whether the lost information is acceptable depends on the task. A task about whether any large response exists in a region may benefit from a maximum; a task requiring exact positions may need the unpooled map or another representation. Do not assume smaller always means better.

blocks.label: A teammate says a 2 by 2 max-pooled map lets them reconstruct the original 4 by 4 map exactly and guarantees unchanged predictions after any one-pixel shift. Use one collision and one boundary example to challenge those claims.

blocks.text: Compare pooling choices with matched data splits and a declared evaluation rule. Fit model parameters on training data and choose alternatives using validation data, leaving final tests reserved. Next week combines these components in a small image-model experiment.

workbook.title: Calculate both summaries
workbook.prompt: For the lesson window starting at [2, 2], list the four values, sum, maximum and mean. State the complete pooled output shape.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Values are 1, 3, 2 and 7. Sum is 13, maximum 7 and mean 3.25. Each pooled output has shape 2 by 2.

workbook.title: Prove that location can be lost
workbook.prompt: Give two different 2 by 2 windows containing exactly one 4 and three zeros that have the same maximum and mean. Explain why either scalar alone cannot identify the position of the 4.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For example, [[4, 0], [0, 0]] and [[0, 4], [0, 0]] both give maximum 4 and mean 1. A deterministic head receiving the same scalar must give the same output, so it cannot distinguish those positions.

workbook.title: Audit an omitted border
workbook.prompt: Apply the lesson complete-window rule to [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4, 99], [99, 99, 99]]. Give the output shape and both outputs. Explain why neither output includes 99.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Shape is 1 by 1. Only [[1, 2], [3, 4]] is read, giving maximum 4 and mean 2.5. The final row and column lie outside the only complete stride-2 window.

workbook.title: Pool a new map independently
workbook.prompt: Use rows [-4, -1, 2, 6], [-3, -2, 4, 0], [5, 1, -8, -2], [3, 7, -4, -6]. Under the lesson rule, give all four sums, the max map and the mean map. Explain why replacing a negative maximum by zero is an error here.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Window sums in row order are -10, 12, 16 and -20. Max map is [[-1, 6], [7, -2]]. Mean map is [[-2.5, 3], [4, -5]]. Zero is not in either all-negative window; pooling is not ReLU and must return the largest actual value.

workbook.title: Check the movement boundary
workbook.prompt: A 2 by 4 map is zero except for 8 at row 0 column 1. Move the 8 to column 2 and set its old position to zero. Give the max and mean maps before and after. What claim does this refute?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Before: max [[8, 0]], mean [[2, 0]]. After: max [[0, 8]], mean [[0, 2]]. Crossing a pooling boundary changes the output, refuting guaranteed invariance to every one-pixel movement.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Prepare a labelled 4 by 4 grid with four window outlines. State complete windows, stride 2 and no padding before any arithmetic. Keep pooling separate from ReLU, and discuss loss of location through explicit collisions. Reference for the floor-based pooling convention: https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.modules.pooling.MaxPool2d.html . No software library is required.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve valid window starts and mark the four nonoverlapping regions.
Calculate both summaries in the first region, then complete W1.
Trace the remaining regions and run or hand-trace the optional code.
Use W2 and the visual to distinguish lost location from retained regional arrangement.
Complete the guided collision and discuss why storing a maximum position is still insufficient for reconstruction.
Use W3 to expose the omitted border, then trace the movement counterexample in W5.
Collect W4 independently, requiring signed sums and both maps without applying ReLU.
Use the exit response to qualify claims, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: both windows have maximum 6 and mean 1.5. Either scalar alone cannot distinguish their different nonzero positions. Exit: the first two visual windows collide, so exact reconstruction is impossible from the pooled values alone. The 8 crossing from column 1 to column 2 changes the pooled map, so universal shift invariance does not follow.
misconceptions: Max pooling turns negative numbers into zero
That is a ReLU behaviour, not the maximum of an all-negative window.
A local pooled grid retains coarse regional arrangement while losing within-window detail.
Saving the maximum position restores the input
Other values remain unknown even when a unique maximum location is recorded.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires sums -10, 12, 16, -20, max map [[-1, 6], [7, -2]] and mean map [[-2.5, 3], [4, -5]]. Fresh retry: rows [-6, -2, 1, 5] and [-4, -8, 3, 7]. Output shape is 1 by 2. Sums are -20 and 16; max map is [[-2, 7]] and mean map is [[-5, 4]]. Require a signed maximum rather than a zero-clamped answer.
teacher.support: Provide separate columns for window values, sum, divisor, maximum and mean. Use numbered positions rather than colour alone. Extension: enumerate all sixteen binary 2 by 2 windows, group them by maximum and mean, and identify collisions under each summary.
